name: Romulus
summary: Legendary founder and first king of Rome; traditionally credited with founding the Senate and army.
contested: Wholly legendary founding figure; Livy and Dionysius wrote centuries after the events, and modern scholarship treats his existence and reign as myth, not history.
date_agreement: matches: source gives 753-716 BC; explicitly calls Romulus 'the legendary Romulus' and states the whole traditional chronology (243 years total, ~35-year average reigns) 'has been generally discounted by modern scholarship' since Niebuhr, and that 'no contemporary records of the kingdom surviving, all accounts of the Roman kings must be carefully questioned.'

name: Numa Pompilius
summary: Second king of Rome; credited with founding Roman religious institutions and the calendar.
contested: Legendary Sabine successor to Romulus; no contemporary evidence, and his 43-year reign is part of a traditional chronology modern historians discount as schematic.
date_agreement: matches: source gives 715-672 BC (43-year reign) and treats the whole regnal chronology, codified by Varro and Fabius Pictor at 243 years total for seven kings, as discounted by modern scholarship since Barthold Georg Niebuhr.

name: Tullus Hostilius
summary: Third king of Rome; credited with destroying Alba Longa and absorbing its nobility into Rome.
contested: Legendary warrior-king whose 32-year reign belongs to the same schematic Livian chronology that modern scholarship regards as unreliable and largely unverifiable.
date_agreement: matches: source gives 672-640 BC, 32-year reign, and reiterates that with no contemporary records surviving from the kingdom, 'all accounts of the Roman kings must be carefully questioned.'

name: Ancus Marcius
summary: Fourth king of Rome; founded the port of Ostia and is traditionally the last of the Latin-Sabine kings.
contested: Legendary figure whose death marks 'the end of Rome's Latin-Sabine kings' per the source, a schematic division scholars treat as narrative structure, not history.
date_agreement: differs: some tellings (e.g. the Wikipedia 'King of Rome' summary table and other tertiary sites) give 640-616 BC as a 24-year reign, while the Roman Kingdom article's own body text describes a 25-year reign ending at his natural death; both fall within the same traditional Livian chronology and neither is an archaeological date.

name: Lucius Tarquinius Priscus
summary: Fifth king of Rome and first of Etruscan birth; expanded the Senate and built the Circus Maximus and Cloaca Maxima.
contested: First king the source explicitly marks as Etruscan rather than Latin-Sabine; scholars regard him as more plausible than the earliest kings but still part of an unattested, retrojected chronology.
date_agreement: matches: source gives 616-578 BC and describes him as 'the fifth king of Rome and the first of Etruscan birth,' the point at which the source begins distinguishing the more historically plausible Etruscan kings from the earlier legendary ones.

name: Servius Tullius
summary: Sixth king of Rome; Etruscan-born reformer credited with the census-based Servian constitution and city walls.
contested: Second Etruscan-birth king per the source; an alternate tradition recorded by Claudius identifies him with a warlord, Mastarna, which historian Momigliano treats as too different to simply merge.
date_agreement: matches: source gives 578-534 BC (44-year reign) and calls him 'Rome's second king of Etruscan birth,' while flagging the competing Mastarna tradition as a genuine historiographical complication rather than a settled identification.

name: Lucius Tarquinius Superbus
summary: Seventh and last king of Rome; his overthrow traditionally marks the founding of the Republic in 509 BCE.
contested: Last traditional king; Tacitus, Pliny, and scholars like Tim Cornell suggest Etruscan king Porsena actually took Rome and ended the monarchy directly, complicating the 'overthrow by Romans' story.
date_agreement: matches: source gives 534-509 BC (25-year reign) and 509 BC as the end of the monarchy, while noting an alternative tradition in which Porsena, not a popular uprising, ended the kingship.

name: Scipio Africanus
summary: Won Roman command in Spain as a private citizen, then as consul defeated Hannibal at Zama, ending the Second Punic War.
date_agreement: differs: dates given span his Spanish command through his Africanus cognomen (210 to 201 BCE); Britannica states he received his Spanish command in 210 BCE as a private citizen ('privatus'), was elected consul for 205 BCE, defeated Hannibal at Zama in 202 BCE, and won the surname Africanus in 201 BCE, so no single office year covers his full significance.

name: Tiberius Gracchus
summary: As tribune, forced through land reform to restore small farmers, triggering the political violence that opened the Republic's crisis.
date_agreement: matches: used his single year as tribune of the plebs (133 BCE) rather than his lifespan (c. 169-164?-133 BCE, per Britannica), since the brief calls for office/command years.

name: Gaius Gracchus
summary: As tribune, extended his brother's land reform and created a subsidized grain supply, deepening the populares-optimates split.
date_agreement: differs: used his two-year tribunate (123-122 BCE) as the office span, but extended the end year to 121 BCE (his death, per Britannica) to mark when the political crisis he provoked was resolved by force; his lifespan is separately given as c. 160-153?-121 BCE.

name: Gaius Marius
summary: Held the consulship seven times and opened the legions to the landless, making armies loyal to commanders rather than the state.
date_agreement: matches: Britannica states he was 'consul seven times (107, 104-100, 86 bce)'; span covers his first to last consulship rather than his lifespan (c. 157-86 BCE).

name: Sulla
summary: Marched on Rome, won the first Roman civil war, and ruled as dictator, reshaping the constitution to entrench senatorial power.
date_agreement: matches: span covers his first consulship and command against Mithradates (88 BCE) through his resignation as dictator (79 BCE); Britannica separately gives his dictatorship alone as 82-79 BCE and his lifespan as 138-78 BCE.

name: Pompey
summary: Cleared the Mediterranean of pirates, defeated Mithradates under extraordinary commands, then became Rome's sole consul.
date_agreement: matches: span runs from his first consulship (70 BCE) to his sole consulship (52 BCE), per Britannica's Quick Facts office list (consul 70, 55, 52 BCE); his extraordinary anti-pirate command (67 BCE) and Mithradatic command (66 BCE) fall inside this range. His lifespan (106-48 BCE) is not used.

name: Marcus Licinius Crassus
summary: Financed rising politicians and crushed the Spartacus revolt, then bankrolled the First Triumvirate that sidelined the Senate.
date_agreement: matches: span runs from his suppression of the Spartacus revolt (72-71 BCE, ending 71) to his death on the disastrous Parthian invasion he launched as governor of Syria (54-53 BCE, ending 53); Britannica also lists consulships in 70 and 55 BCE within that span. Lifespan (c. 115-53 BCE) is not used.

name: Cicero
summary: As consul, exposed and crushed the Catiline conspiracy, then became the Republic's foremost voice defending constitutional government.
date_agreement: matches: used his consulship (63 BCE), the year Britannica says he 'discover[ed] and ma[de] public the seditious intentions of Catiline'; his lifespan (106-43 BCE) and later governorship of Cilicia (51-50 BCE) are not used as the primary date.

name: Julius Caesar
summary: Conquered Gaul, won the civil war against Pompey, and ruled as dictator, ending collective senatorial government in all but name.
date_agreement: matches: span runs from his first consulship (59 BCE) to his assassination while dictator (44 BCE); Britannica separately breaks this into conquest of Gaul (58-50 BCE), civil war victory (49-45 BCE), and dictatorship (46-44 BCE). Lifespan (100-44 BCE) is not used as the office span.

name: Cato the Younger
summary: As tribune and senator, led principled Senate resistance to Caesar and Pompey, and chose suicide at Utica over living under Caesar's rule.
date_agreement: differs: used his tenure of major office, from plebeian tribune (62 BCE) to his death commanding the last Republican resistance at Utica (46 BCE), rather than the page's own 'Years active' field, which is given as 67-46 BCE (starting from his military tribunate); his praetorship (54 BCE) also falls within the chosen span. Lifespan is 95-46 BCE.

name: Mark Antony
summary: Seized Caesar's legacy, ruled the eastern Mediterranean as triumvir with Cleopatra, and lost Rome's last civil war to Octavian.
date_agreement: matches: Britannica identifies him as 'triumvir (43-30 bce)'; start year adjusted to 44 BCE to include his consulship the year Caesar was assassinated, which the source treats as the start of his rise to power. Lifespan (c. 83-30 BCE) is not used.

name: Octavian
summary: Won the Second Triumvirate's power struggle and Actium, then formally 'restored' the Republic while keeping real power as princeps.
date_agreement: matches: span covers his consulship and formation of the Second Triumvirate (43 BCE, per Britannica's Quick Facts 'triumvirate (43BC-32BC)') through 27 BCE, when Britannica states he 'restored the republic of Rome' and was granted the name Augustus, becoming emperor; entry stops at 27 BCE per the brief's instruction not to duplicate the Empire dataset.
